# Task: Explain the fixed SSA method and UTKFace setup

Write an original 450–650 word methods explanation using only the facts below. Do not reproduce source phrasing. Cover (1) why ordinary feature alignment is problematic for regression, (2) source statistics and subspace detection, (3) weighting and target alignment loss, and (4) the UTKFace corruption setup. Clearly label the setup as the paper’s reported experiment, not a new result of this writing task. Do not report performance numbers or use Table 1/4 outcomes.

## Fixed method specification

A source-trained regressor has features z=g_phi(x) in R^D and scalar head h_psi(z)=w^T z+b. The source feature mean is mu^s=(1/N_s) sum_{i=1}^{N_s} z_i^s. Its covariance is Sigma^s=(1/N_s) sum_i (z_i^s-mu^s)(z_i^s-mu^s)^T (Eq. 5). Let (lambda_k^s,v_k^s) be covariance eigenpairs, with unit eigenvectors and eigenvalues ordered descending. The detected source basis V^s contains the top K eigenvectors; their eigenvalues are lambda_1^s,...,lambda_K^s. In this task K is described only for the UTKFace setting below.

For each selected direction d, the importance weight is alpha_d=1+|w^T v_d^s| (Eq. 6). Thus relevance is measured through the linear prediction head’s coefficient along that basis direction. For target feature z_i^t, project and center using source statistics: z_tilde_i^t=V^s(z_i^t-mu^s) (Eq. 7). From target projected coordinates estimate per-coordinate mean mu_tilde_d^t and variance sigma_tilde_d^{t 2}; source projected coordinates are centered and have variance lambda_d^s. The paper’s Eq. 8 loss is the weighted sum of coordinate-wise Gaussian KL divergences, with target N(mu_tilde_d^t,sigma_tilde_d^{t 2}) and source N(0,lambda_d^s):

L = (1/2) sum_{d=1}^K alpha_d [ ((mu_tilde_d^t)^2+lambda_d^s)/sigma_tilde_d^{t 2} + ((mu_tilde_d^t)^2+sigma_tilde_d^{t 2})/lambda_d^s - 2 ].

Explain this as distribution alignment in the detected subspace. Do not invent optimizers, update rules, batch sizes, regularization, or numerical safeguards absent from these facts. The equation presumes positive variances; do not imply how zero/near-zero target variance is handled.

## Reported UTKFace setting

The paper reports ResNet-50 for UTKFace; its penultimate features have 2048 dimensions. The source model is trained on original images. Target corruption uses 13 ImageNet-C corruption types at severity level five. The default subspace dimension is K=100.

## Output and evidence rules

Use headings: Motivation and setup; Subspace detection; Dimension weighting and alignment; UTKFace instantiation; Precision limits. Cite fact IDs inline: C-MOT, C-COV, C-WEIGHT, C-LOSS, C-UTK. Preserve symbols/conditions and distinguish source statements from any paraphrased interpretation. Mention the variance positivity limitation. No citations to external sources are needed. This is an exposition task, not an experiment or a claim to reproduce the authors’ reasoning.

"""Render Table 4 UTKFace corruption R^2 values from the accompanying CSV."""
import argparse, csv
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def render(data_path, output_path):
    with open(data_path, newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        rows=list(csv.DictReader(f))
    methods=[r['Method'] for r in rows]
    columns=list(rows[0].keys())[1:-1]
    vals=[[float(r[c]) for c in columns] for r in rows]
    fig, ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(13,5.8), constrained_layout=True)
    im=ax.imshow(vals,aspect='auto',cmap='coolwarm',vmin=-4.5,vmax=1.0)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(columns)),columns,rotation=45,ha='right')
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(methods)),methods)
    ax.set_title('UTKFace test $R^2$ under image corruption (Table 4)')
    ax.set_xlabel('Corruption type (13 types; severity level five in reported setup)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Method')
    fig.colorbar(im,ax=ax,label='Test $R^2$ (unitless)')
    fig.savefig(output_path,dpi=160)
    plt.close(fig)

if __name__=='__main__':
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser(); p.add_argument('--data',default='table4_utkface.csv'); p.add_argument('--output',default='table4_heatmap.png'); a=p.parse_args(); render(a.data,a.output)

For feature alignment, we seek to make the target statistics similar to the source ones. For this purpose, we use the KL divergence as Nguyen et al. [45] proved that it is included in an upper bound of the target error in unsupervised domain adaptation. Concretely, we minimize the KL divergence between two diagonal Gaussian distributions 𝒩⁡(𝝁s,𝝈s 2)\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}},{\bm{\sigma}^{\text{s~2}}}) and 𝒩⁡(𝝁^t,𝝈^t 2)\mathcal{N}(\hat{\bm{\mu}}^{\text{t}},\hat{\bm{\sigma}}^{\text{t~2}}):

where the subscripts dd represent the dd-th elements of the mean and variance vectors. Here, we used both directions of the KL divergence because it empirically had good results as recommended by Nguyen et al. [45]. The KL divergence between two univariate Gaussians can be written in a closed form [15]

DKL\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}} (𝒩(μ1,σ12)∥𝒩(μ2,σ22))\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{N}(\mu_{1},\sigma_{1}^{2})\|\mathcal{N}(\mu_{2},\sigma_{2}^{2})\right)

However, in regression models, the features tend to be less diverse than in classification [58]. In addition to the insight from Zhang et al. [58], we observed that the features of a regression model trained on 𝒮\mathcal{S} are distributed in only a small subspace of the feature space and many dimensions of the feature space had zero variances. Tab. 1 shows the numbers of valid (having non-zero variance) feature dimensions and feature subspace dimensions (see Sec. 4.3.1 for more details). This property makes the naive feature alignment described above unstable since the KL divergence in Eq. 4 includes the variance in the denominator. Also, this naive feature alignment is ineffective because many of the feature dimensions have a small effect on the subspace.

3.2 Significant-subspace Alignment

In this section, we describe our method, Significant-subspace Alignment (SSA), to tackle the aforementioned problem of naive feature alignment. Fig. 1 shows an overview of SSA. As described in Sec. 3.1, the features of a regression model tend to be distributed in a small subspace of the feature space. Thus, we introduce subspace detection to detect a subspace that is representative and significant to the output and then perform feature alignment in the subspace. Subspace detection is similar to principal component analysis (PCA). Further, in our regression model, a feature 𝐳=gϕ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) is projected onto a one-dimensional line determined by 𝐰\mathbf{w} of hψh_{\psi} in order to output a scalar value 𝐰⊤​𝐳+b\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}+b. Thus, a subspace basis 𝐯ds\mathbf{v}^{\text{s}}_{d} whose direction is not orthogonal to 𝐰\mathbf{w} needs precise feature alignment. We use dimension weighting to prioritize such dimensions.

Subspace detection. After the training on the source dataset 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we detect the subspace in which the source features are distributed. Instead of computing the variance of each dimension as Eqs. 1 and 2, we compute the covariance matrix:

𝚺s=1Ns​∑i=1Ns(𝐳is−𝝁s)​(𝐳is−𝝁s)⊤,\bm{\Sigma}^{\text{s}}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{s}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{s}}}(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{s}}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}})(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{s}}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}})^{\top}, (5)

where the source mean vector 𝝁s\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}} is the same as Eqs. 1 and 2.

Then, we detect the source subspace. On the basis of PCA, the subspace is spanned by the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix 𝚺s\bm{\Sigma}^{\text{s}}, denoted by 𝐯ks\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}} (‖𝐯ks‖2=1\|\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}\|_{2}=1). The corresponding eigenvalues λks\lambda_{k}^{\text{s}} represent the variance of the source features along the direction 𝐯ks\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}. We use the top-KK largest eigenvalues λ1s,…,λKs​(λ1s>⋯>λKs)\lambda_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\lambda_{K}^{\text{s}}~(\lambda_{1}^{\text{s}}>\cdots>\lambda_{K}^{\text{s}}), the corresponding source bases 𝐯1s,…,𝐯Ks\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{K}^{\text{s}}, and the source mean 𝝁s\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}} as the source statistics.
